A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPCA work by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original Gaussian simulations and learned geodesic results for MNIST, ModelNet40 point clouds and landscape images.

after.justification: Original empirical results include the retained applications, new weather and outlier-detection experiments, point-cloud baseline comparisons and quantitative regularization studies.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces the Wasserstein intersection penalty between distributions with squared distance between lifted maps, enforcing a shared representative for the orthogonality calculation. Sections 3 and D.2 also fix redundant Gaussian rotation variables to the identity. These refine the existing algorithms while retaining their principal objectives and neural parameterization.

E1.justification: v2 adds Weather CORGIS covariance analysis and an outlier-detection task using held-out chairs versus cars and planes. These extend the represented domain, object categories and task requirements beyond the retained Gaussian, MNIST, chair/lamp and landscape experiments.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates TPCA against GPCA in Gaussian examples. v2 additionally evaluates TPCA on the retained chair/lamp experiments and introduces pretrained PointNet embeddings followed by PCA as another comparator (Appendix A.2, Figures 15–17), substantially expanding comparisons for GPCAGEN.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the projection-time learning rate from 0.001 to 0.005, and Appendix E revises its search grid. New evaluation designs include controlled regularization sweeps and held-out outlier scoring using 20 projection-time candidates and 2048 samples per candidate. The main network architectures and 120,000/200,000-step training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 provides informal regularization observations and a tuning-grid description. v2 adds controlled lamp experiments varying each regularization weight from 0.001 to 100 while fixing the other, measuring constraint satisfaction and component loss and displaying recovered geodesics (Tables 2–3, Figures 20–21). The new scalability sections discuss possible remedies rather than report scaling experiments.

E5.justification: Figure 4 changes from retaining the best of five runs to averaging ten runs with a standard-deviation band. Appendix E.2 introduces ± statistics and reports 100 runs for constraint measurement and five for cost measurement; these counts do not establish independent retraining runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds weather embeddings, baseline outputs, outlier-score histograms and numerical ablation results. For example, Table 2 newly reports orthogonality values of 0.909 at lambda_O=0.001 and 0.00031 at lambda_O=1. The reported chair modes also reverse order: chair-versus-armchair variation becomes the first component and seat height the second.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 repairs the SPD-cone inequality and its matching covariance parameterization, and the main distortion proposition gains a nonzero-rotation condition. The distortion expansion and univariate Gaussian preservation result, including their proofs, already appear in v1; their relocation and renumbering do not constitute new theory.

C1.justification: The central claims about two algorithms for exact Wasserstein GPCA remain. v2 broadens the discussion's stated utility to classification, clustering and outlier detection, and highlights the existing univariate Gaussian result in the contribution list. This is a limited expansion and reframing of the contribution scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments about comparator suitability, discretization artifacts and encoder geometry, interpretations of the regularization studies, and limitations of estimating Hessian extrema in high dimensions. One new interpretation overstates its evidence: Appendix E.2.2 says increasing lambda_I does not harm cost, although Table 3 increases from 5.76 at weight 1 to 5.91 at weight 100.

D1.justification: v2 documents access to two implementation repositories, identifies the pretrained PointNet source, supplies the POT-based outlier-scoring recipe and adds a reproducibility statement. It also revises learning-rate documentation. Most architecture, optimizer, hardware and training-budget information was already supplied in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning Sinkhorn methods, PointNet, LOBPCG and convex analysis, alongside targeted discussion of encoder-based PCA and alternative SPD geometries. The central positioning against tangent PCA and generalized-geodesic approximations remains; the switch to author-year citations is primarily presentational.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative and most proof text are retained. v2 rewrites introductory passages, adds a related-work paragraph, moves the distortion proposition into Section 3 and subdivides Appendices A and E. It also adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements, while accidentally repeating the title at the start of the abstract.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, including narrower text blocks and text wrapped around several figures. It substantially expands the visual evidence with weather, baseline, outlier and ablation displays plus Tables 2–3. Existing plots are updated, Figure 4 gains an uncertainty band, and retained appendix figures are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the technical and empirical support for GPCAGEN. The revised intersection constraint aligns the lifted representatives used to assess orthogonality, while controlled ablations replace informal tuning assertions with measured constraint and loss tradeoffs. Baseline comparisons, averaged results with uncertainty and documented code access improve validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh limited reporting inconsistencies such as the overstatement accompanying Table 3, although baseline comparisons remain chiefly qualitative.
